cards.title: Top of the Ladder
cards.instruction: Carry yourself as the highest-status person present. Treat questions as requests for your approval.

cards.title: Pick the Prize
cards.instruction: Make them choose which reward, principle, or relationship matters most when not everything can be kept.

beats.speaker: A
beats.text: I'll decide how we handle this. You can keep the prize money or fund the team trip. Which matters more?

beats.speaker: B
beats.text: Can't we do a cheaper trip?

beats.speaker: A
beats.text: You can question the details after my decision. Only if someone adds money. You hold the prize.

beats.speaker: A
beats.text: I'm asking you to choose before everyone else quietly pays for it.

cardFidelity.evidence: A1 sets keep-prize/fund-trip choice, A3 conditions B2 cheaper option on other funding, A5 refuses B4 reputation objection as reason to obscure who pays; authority defines the acceptable explicit choice.

responseLogic.evidence: B2 cheaper trip causes A3 funding-source question; B4 selfish appearance causes A5 other people quietly bearing cost.

relationship.evidence: B2 seeks compromise and B4 worries about social judgment, credible reactions to public money pressure.

heightening.evidence: A5 uses B4 reputation concern to force recognition of cost transfer, deepening the existing priority choice.

specificity.evidence: A1 prize money and team trip establish resources; A3 B holds prize explains why keeping it leaves another payer.

brevityWit.evidence: A3 generic preface is redundant; A5 quietly pays follows the unresolved funding, not a detached moral.
